sentence: Looking at the quarter, we drove meaningful top-line acceleration through disciplined execution against our North Star metrics. Operating leverage continues to expand as we lean into our highest-ROI initiatives and rationalize the long tail of underperforming SKUs. We're seeing strong tailwinds in our enterprise segment, with net retention ticking up sequentially. Going forward, we'll continue to operationalize our go-to-market motion and double-click on the cohorts driving outsized LTV.

We're pleased to report that EBITDA expansion outpaced consensus, driven by structural cost takeouts and a favorable mix shift toward higher-margin offerings. Synergies from the integration are tracking ahead of plan, and we've identified incremental opportunities to harvest efficiencies as we sunset legacy platforms. Capital allocation remains disciplined, with a clear bias toward organic reinvestment in our highest-conviction bets.

Bookings velocity remained robust despite a choppier macro, and we're seeing healthy momentum across our flagship verticals. The investments we've made in our platform are paying dividends, with attach rates climbing as customers consolidate spend with strategic partners. We're laser-focused on driving durable, profitable growth and expect operating margins to inflect positively as we scale into our fixed cost base.

On a constant-currency basis, we delivered double-digit growth while expanding free cash flow conversion meaningfully. Our pricing actions are flowing through cleanly, and we're seeing limited churn as customers internalize the value proposition. Looking out to next year, we feel good about the setup: strong pipeline coverage, healthy win rates, and a product roadmap that's resonating with the C-suite buyer.

We continue to take a balanced approach to capital deployment, with M&A optionality remaining a key lever as we evaluate bolt-on assets that are accretive to our strategic flywheel. The team has done exceptional work pulling forward the synergy timeline, and we're now guiding to the high end of our previously communicated range. This is a multi-year compounding story and we remain bullish on the secular tailwinds underpinning our category.

Net-net, we're executing against a clear playbook and the results speak for themselves. We've materially de-risked the transformation and are now in harvest mode on the productivity initiatives announced at our investor day. The flywheel is gaining momentum, unit economics are improving, and we have line of sight to our medium-term margin algorithm. We thank our colleagues for their relentless focus on driving shareholder value.

ARR growth re-accelerated this quarter as our enterprise motion gained traction and we landed several lighthouse logos that validate the upmarket thesis. Gross retention held firmly above ninety percent, and we're driving meaningful expansion within the installed base through cross-sell of our adjacent modules. The data continues to underscore the strength of our category position.

We're seeing a pivot in customer behavior toward consolidation of vendors, which plays directly into our integrated platform narrative. Deal sizes are trending up, sales cycles are normalizing, and our enterprise pipeline is the healthiest it's been in eight quarters. We feel well-positioned heading into next year and are reaffirming our long-term financial framework.

Stepping back, the through-line of this quarter is operational discipline meeting a strengthening demand environment. We've right-sized the cost base, deepened our moat through differentiated R&D investment, and built a flywheel that's increasingly self-reinforcing. Cash conversion remains best-in-class and the balance sheet gives us substantial dry powder for opportunistic capital deployment.

Looking through the quarter-to-quarter noise, the underlying KPIs all point in the right direction. Customer acquisition costs are compressing, payback periods are shortening, and lifetime value continues to march higher as we deepen the product surface area. We have conviction in our long-range plan and are committed to delivering top-quartile returns through the cycle.

Coming out of the offsite, the leadership team aligned around three big bets that will define our next chapter. We need to ruthlessly prioritize, kill the zombies, and concentrate firepower behind the initiatives that genuinely move the needle. The strategic narrative has to be tight, the OKRs cascading, and every function laddering up to the same enterprise outcomes.

We spent two days pressure-testing the strategy and the conclusion is clear: we've been over-indexed on incremental optimization and under-invested in horizon-three optionality. The path forward requires bolder bets, faster decision velocity, and a willingness to sunset sacred cows. We're going to operationalize this by carving out a dedicated SWAT team with a mandate to disrupt ourselves before someone else does.

The offsite surfaced some uncomfortable truths about organizational friction and unclear decision rights. We agreed to clean up the RACI, collapse layers where appropriate, and push accountability closer to the customer. Empowered teams with clear guardrails will outperform centralized command-and-control every time, and we need to model that from the top.

We workshopped the three-year plan and stress-tested it against multiple macro scenarios. The takeaway: our strategy is robust to most downside cases as long as we maintain pricing discipline and don't lose focus on our highest-conviction segments. We'll reconvene in six weeks to socialize the refined narrative with the broader leadership cohort.

Strategy without execution is hallucination. The offsite was productive, but the real work begins now: translating these high-level themes into a crisp set of must-win battles, each with a clear owner, milestone plan, and success criteria. We need to build the operating cadence to drive accountability and surface blockers in near-real-time.

One of the most valuable conversations centered on our right-to-win in adjacent categories. We mapped the strategic landscape, identified where our capabilities give us asymmetric advantage, and aligned on a build-buy-partner framework to accelerate entry. The team left energized and with a shared sense of urgency around the prize.

We did a deep-dive on the competitive landscape and concluded that our differentiation is real but not always well-articulated. There's a clear opportunity to sharpen our value proposition, ladder it back to customer pain points, and ensure the entire commercial organization is selling the same story. Marketing will own this workstream end-to-end.

The strategic refresh confirmed that our flywheel is intact but needs to spin faster. We're going to invest behind the demand generation engine, tighten the funnel handoffs, and instrument the customer journey end-to-end. Data-driven decisioning has to become the default, not the exception, and we need to build the muscle to act on signal rather than gut feel.

We tabled several second-order workstreams to maintain focus on the critical few. Saying no to good ideas to say yes to great ones is the hardest part of strategy, but it's where leadership has to lean in. The portfolio is now stack-ranked, resourcing is being reallocated, and the executive team is fully bought in.

The offsite outputs will be socialized through a series of town halls, working sessions, and one-on-ones over the next four weeks. We need to win hearts and minds, not just align on the slide deck. Culture eats strategy for breakfast, and the team has to feel ownership of the path forward, not just compliance with it.

Walking through the OKR scorecard, we're trending green on the customer acquisition objective but yellow on the activation key result. The team has identified the root cause as friction in the onboarding flow and is shipping a redesigned experience next sprint. We expect to course-correct and land in the seventy-to-seventy-five percent attainment range, which is squarely in the ambitious-but-achievable zone.

Our north star OKR around platform stickiness is showing real progress, with weekly active usage up meaningfully against baseline. That said, we need to interrogate whether the key results actually capture the underlying outcome, or if we're optimizing for proxies. The team will refresh the measurement framework in the next planning cycle to ensure we're not gaming our own scorecard.

Several OKRs are at risk and we need to triage. The recommendation is to descope the two stretch objectives that are no longer well-aligned with current strategic priorities and concentrate resources on the foundational ones. Better to overdeliver on a tight set than to spread thin across an unrealistic portfolio. The exec team should bless the rebaselining by Friday.

Looking at the cross-functional OKRs, there's a clear dependency bottleneck on the data infrastructure team. Their deliverables are blocking three downstream objectives, so we need to escalate resourcing and potentially pull in contractor capacity to unblock. This is a textbook case where the org structure is impeding the operating model and we need to surface it to the leadership team.

The OKR check-in highlighted strong attainment on retention metrics but a gap on monetization. The thesis was that activation would drive monetization downstream, but the funnel data suggests a weaker conversion link than modeled. We need to revisit the assumptions and potentially decouple the objectives next quarter to drive sharper accountability.

Quarter-over-quarter, our OKR hit rate has improved from sixty-two to seventy-eight percent. That's a meaningful inflection and reflects the discipline we've built around scoping ambitious-but-credible targets. The cultural shift toward outcomes over outputs is taking hold, and we're seeing more rigorous trade-off conversations at the team level.

There's a healthy tension between aspirational OKRs and committed roadmap, and we need to be intentional about how we frame it. Stretch objectives should be genuine moonshots where seventy percent attainment is a win, while committed key results should be operational table stakes. Conflating the two erodes accountability and creates sandbagging dynamics.

We need to instrument the leading indicators more rigorously so we're not surprised at quarter-end. Right now too many OKRs are scored on lagging measures, which means we lose the ability to course-correct mid-quarter. The recommendation is to identify one leading proxy per key result and review it weekly in the operating cadence.

The OKR portfolio is healthy overall but a couple of teams are clearly under-scoping. When everyone's at ninety-plus percent attainment, the targets weren't ambitious enough. We should encourage more swing-for-the-fences thinking and reward intelligent failure, otherwise we're optimizing the org for comfort rather than impact.

Closing the loop on last quarter's OKRs, we landed at sixty-eight percent overall attainment, which is in the healthy stretch zone. The lessons learned will inform next quarter's planning: tighter dependency mapping, more conservative resourcing assumptions, and a sharper distinction between input and outcome metrics. The teams have done excellent work and the muscle is getting stronger.

Our digital transformation journey is foundationally about re-architecting the business for a cloud-native, data-first, AI-enabled future. We've made meaningful progress decomposing the monolith, modernizing the tech stack, and embedding product thinking across the enterprise. The next leg requires us to operationalize a true platform mindset and unlock the network effects of our data assets.

The transformation roadmap is anchored on four strategic pillars: customer experience, operational excellence, employee enablement, and platform modernization. Each pillar has a clear executive sponsor, a multi-year investment thesis, and a portfolio of initiatives with measurable business outcomes. Governance happens through a quarterly steering committee that ruthlessly prioritizes against value-at-stake.

We're moving from a project-based delivery model to a product operating model, which is a fundamental shift in how value gets created and measured. Cross-functional pods, durable ownership, and outcome-based KPIs replace the traditional waterfall handoffs. The change management lift is real but the operating leverage on the other side is substantial.

Legacy technical debt remains our biggest drag on velocity, and we've committed to a multi-year modernization program to systematically retire it. The business case is compelling: every dollar invested in platform hygiene unlocks roughly three dollars of downstream productivity through faster cycle times and lower change-failure rates. This is foundational, not optional.

Data is the connective tissue of the transformation. Without trusted, accessible, well-governed data, every downstream initiative slows to a crawl. We're standing up a centralized data platform, instituting clear stewardship roles, and embedding data literacy across the workforce. The objective is to make every employee a citizen analyst empowered to act on signal in their domain.

AI is the force multiplier that will accelerate every dimension of the transformation. We're embedding AI capabilities into core workflows, augmenting decision-making, and reimagining customer touchpoints. The principle is human-in-the-loop, governed deployment, and a relentless focus on use cases with measurable ROI rather than vanity demonstrations.

Transformation fatigue is a real risk and we need to manage the change capacity of the organization deliberately. Sequencing matters: too many concurrent initiatives create cognitive overload, blur priorities, and ultimately erode trust. We're tightening the portfolio gate and forcing trade-offs upstream rather than letting them surface as execution misses downstream.

The cultural dimension of transformation is harder than the technical one. We're investing in capability building, evolving incentive structures, and modeling new behaviors at the top. You cannot rewire an enterprise without rewiring its mental models, and that takes intentionality, repetition, and visible executive sponsorship over a sustained period.

We're benchmarking ourselves against best-in-class digital natives across cycle time, deployment frequency, and customer NPS. The gap is closing but remains material in certain domains. The path forward is to relentlessly study what world-class looks like, import the practices that translate, and resist the temptation to declare victory prematurely.

Two years into the transformation, we're at the inflection point where the foundational investments start compounding. Time-to-market has compressed by forty percent on instrumented workflows, customer satisfaction is trending up, and the developer experience has materially improved. The flywheel is turning, and the next phase is about scaling the wins horizontally across the enterprise.

Walking through the pipeline, we have healthy top-of-funnel coverage but conversion at the mid-funnel stage is softer than we'd like. The diagnosis is that too many opportunities are getting stuck in commercial validation, often because the economic buyer wasn't engaged early enough. We need to push hard on multi-threading and ensure every six-figure deal has executive sponsorship on both sides.

Our pipeline-to-quota ratio sits at three-point-two-x, which is below our target of four-x for this stage of the quarter. We need to drive aggressive top-of-funnel motion through targeted ABM plays and outbound sequencing. The SDR team is rolling out a new cadence next week aimed at re-engaging dormant accounts and surfacing latent demand.

Looking at deal velocity, our enterprise cycles have stretched by about eleven percent quarter-over-quarter, which tracks with broader buyer scrutiny in the current environment. We're countering with sharper business cases, more rigorous champion enablement, and earlier procurement engagement. The pull-forward strategy is gaining traction on the larger opportunities.

Win rates on competitive deals are up six points, which validates the new sales play and the refreshed competitive battle cards. Where we continue to struggle is in greenfield logos against the incumbent vendor's installed base. The recommendation is to focus the AEs on displacement plays with a structured framework and dedicated overlay resources.

The forecast call surfaced several at-risk deals that need executive air cover this week. We're going to do hand-to-hand combat on the top five must-win opportunities and treat them as cross-functional swarms with engineering, customer success, and finance fully bought in. These are franchise-defining logos and we cannot afford to lose them on details.

Pipeline hygiene continues to be an issue, with too many stale opportunities lingering in the late stages. We're going to enforce a stricter exit criteria policy and aggressively prune anything that hasn't progressed in forty-five days. Better to have a smaller, higher-quality pipeline than to carry inflated numbers that obscure the real signal.

Our average contract value is trending up nicely as we lean into the enterprise segment, but the trade-off is longer cycles and more procurement friction. The commercial framework needs to evolve to support this motion: senior sales talent, deeper deal desk, dedicated solutions consulting. We're making the investments but they take time to compound.

The renewal cohort coming up next quarter represents over forty million in ARR, so we need surgical focus on retention and expansion. Customer success has built individualized success plans for each strategic account, and we're proactively engaging on QBRs to surface adoption risks early. Net retention above one-fifteen is the target.

Discounting discipline has slipped and we need to course-correct. Average realized discount is up three hundred basis points this quarter, which is eroding margin and setting a difficult precedent for renewals. The deal desk needs to clamp down on approvals and we should sunset the legacy discount matrix in favor of value-based pricing principles.

Net-net, we're confident in landing the quarter inside the guided range, but it will require disciplined execution and probably some creative deal structuring on the largest opportunities. We're not going to chase revenue at any cost, but we will lean in hard where the strategic logic supports it. Let's keep the energy high and finish strong.

Team, what an incredible quarter. The energy, the execution, the relentless focus on the customer — it's been extraordinary to watch. We've shipped flagship features, landed marquee logos, and meaningfully strengthened our category leadership. None of this happens without each and every one of you bringing your full selves to work every day. Thank you for what you do.

I want to use this all-hands to recommit to our mission and remind everyone why we're here. We're not in the business of building features; we're in the business of fundamentally transforming how our customers operate. That north star has to inform every decision, every prioritization conversation, every late-night debugging session. Mission-driven companies win, full stop.

There's no sugarcoating it: this past quarter was a tough one. We missed plan, the macro turned against us, and several big bets didn't land the way we hoped. But I want to be clear-eyed about the path forward. We have a generational opportunity in front of us, the right team in the seats, and a balance sheet that gives us runway to execute. We will get through this stronger.

I want to talk transparently about the org changes we announced this morning. These were hard decisions, made with deliberation and a heavy heart. We're focusing our investment on the bets with the highest conviction and that necessarily means saying goodbye to teammates whose contributions we deeply valued. We will support every impacted colleague through this transition with dignity and care.

As we head into the second half, three priorities should anchor every team's planning conversation. One: ruthless customer obsession. Two: operational excellence in everything we ship. Three: building the durable capabilities that compound over time. If a workstream doesn't ladder up to one of these, we should question why it's on the roadmap. Focus is a competitive advantage.

Let me take a moment to recognize the team behind our flagship launch. The cross-functional collaboration was a masterclass: engineering shipped on time, design delivered a magical experience, marketing nailed the narrative, and sales drove pipeline ahead of plan. This is how we win — together, with shared accountability and zero ego in the room.

I want to open the floor for questions in a moment, but first a reflection. The pace of change in our industry has never been faster, and our ability to adapt is our most important muscle. Stay curious, stay humble, stay close to the customer. Comfort is the enemy of growth, both personal and organizational, and we're at our best when we're stretching.

On the strategic update front: we've made meaningful progress against our three-year plan. Platform consolidation is on track, the international expansion is exceeding expectations, and the AI initiative is starting to ship customer-facing value. The compounding is starting to show up in the numbers, and the conviction level among the leadership team has never been higher.

I know there's been a lot of speculation about the leadership changes, so let me address it head-on. We've brought in world-class talent to round out the executive team and accelerate our next phase of growth. Each new leader brings deep domain expertise and a track record of scaling category-defining companies. The bar is rising, and that's exactly what this stage requires.

Closing thought: this is the moment we lean in. The market is consolidating, our competition is stumbling, and our products have never been stronger. History rewards the companies that pour fuel on the fire when others are pulling back. Let's seize this window with both hands and write the next chapter together. Thank you, team.

Our leadership principles are not posters on the wall; they are the operating system of how we lead, decide, and behave. Customer obsession means starting with the customer and working backwards. Bias for action means recognizing that calculated risk-taking is the cost of progress. Insist on the highest standards means refusing to ship anything mediocre. These principles guide us, especially when the path is unclear.

Disagree and commit is one of the most important and least understood principles in our culture. It is not capitulation; it is the recognition that once a decision is made through rigorous debate, the entire leadership team owns it as if they personally chose it. Public alignment, private candor in subsequent reviews. That's the discipline of high-functioning teams.

Ownership is a mindset, not a job description. Leaders take responsibility for outcomes beyond their immediate scope, raise the flag when they see something off, and never say 'that's not my team.' We are one company, one mission, one P&L. Functional silos are organizational artifacts, not excuses for inaction. Every leader is a steward of the whole.

Hire and develop the best. Talent compounds. Every hiring decision is a multi-year investment in the trajectory of the team and the company. Raise the bar with every hire, double down on developing the high performers already in seat, and address performance issues with directness and care. Mediocrity is contagious, and so is excellence; choose what you propagate.

Frugality breeds resourcefulness, self-sufficiency, and invention. Constraints are not obstacles; they are creative forcing functions. The teams that consistently outperform are the ones who treat every dollar of OPEX as if it were their own, who optimize for impact-per-headcount, and who reject the false assumption that more resources equal better outcomes.

Earn trust by listening attentively, speaking candidly, and treating others respectfully. Trust is the lubricant of high-velocity organizations. When trust is high, we can move fast, give direct feedback, and disagree without breaking things. When trust is low, every decision requires expensive coordination overhead and our throughput collapses. Invest in trust deliberately, daily.

Dive deep. Leaders operate at all levels, stay connected to the details, and are skeptical when metrics and anecdote differ. The most dangerous failure mode in a scaling org is leadership becoming abstracted from the actual work. Get into the data. Sit with the customer. Ride along with the support team. Insight lives at the front line.

Have backbone, disagree and commit. Leaders are obligated to respectfully challenge decisions when they disagree, even when doing so is uncomfortable or exhausting. Leaders have conviction and are tenacious. They do not compromise for the sake of social cohesion. Once a decision is determined, however, they commit wholly. Cosmetic agreement followed by sandbagging is corrosive.

Deliver results. We focus on the key inputs for our business and deliver them with the right quality and in a timely fashion. Despite setbacks, we rise to the occasion and never settle. This principle is the integrating capstone: vision without execution is hallucination, and execution without principles is empty motion. We are judged, ultimately, by what we ship and the impact it creates.

Think big. Thinking small is a self-fulfilling prophecy. Leaders create and communicate a bold direction that inspires results. They think differently and look around corners for ways to serve customers. The companies that change the world are led by people who refuse to accept the constraints of conventional wisdom. We aspire to be one of those companies.

The post-mortem on the platform incident surfaced several systemic issues we need to address head-on. Root cause was a cascading dependency failure exacerbated by inadequate runbook coverage and slow incident escalation. The action items include hardening the failover path, instrumenting better observability, and running quarterly chaos engineering drills. Blameless culture remains paramount.

Stepping back from the launch retrospective, the headline learning is that we under-invested in cross-functional alignment in the run-up. Engineering, marketing, and sales had different mental models of the launch timeline, and that drift compounded into the messy week-of execution. Going forward, every tier-one launch will have a dedicated launch lead and a single source of truth for cross-functional dependencies.

The deal slipped because we lost the procurement battle, not the technical evaluation. We had the champion, we had the user love, but we did not engage finance and legal early enough. The lesson is to build a procurement playbook into every enterprise opportunity from stage one, with redlined paper templates, security questionnaires, and references queued up to compress the validation phase.

Honest post-mortem: we got the strategic positioning right and the execution wrong. The category insight was correct, the buyer was real, and the willingness-to-pay was validated. Where we stumbled was in commercial readiness — packaging, pricing, and partner enablement all lagged the GTM motion. We're rebuilding the launch checklist from first principles.

The retrospective on the acquisition integration revealed predictable but painful lessons. We over-indexed on synergy capture and under-invested in culture preservation, which led to attritition of key talent in the first eighteen months. Future integrations will use a more nuanced playbook that explicitly protects critical knowledge holders and gives the acquired team meaningful agency in integration design.

Looking at the failed product launch through a clear-eyed lens, the issue was not the product itself but the go-to-market assumptions baked into the business case. We assumed enterprise procurement velocity that simply doesn't exist in this segment. The lesson: pressure-test the GTM thesis with as much rigor as we pressure-test the product thesis. Both have to be true for the launch to succeed.

The post-incident review identified a chain of small judgment calls that individually seemed reasonable but cumulatively created the conditions for the outage. This is classic Swiss cheese model failure: every layer of defense had a hole, and the holes lined up. We need to treat near-misses as seriously as we treat incidents, because they reveal the same systemic gaps without the customer pain.

We failed to hit the milestone because the dependency map was incomplete and the critical path was misidentified. The team executed against what they thought was the plan, but the actual plan had silent prerequisites that nobody owned. Going forward, every major program will use a formal dependency walk-down at kickoff and again at the midpoint to catch hidden bottlenecks.

Painful but useful learning from the pricing experiment: the willingness-to-pay signal was real, but we didn't anticipate the cannibalization of the legacy tier. The net revenue impact was negative for two quarters before the upsell flywheel kicked in. We should have modeled the transition more rigorously and prepared the finance team for the trough.

Net-net from the post-mortem: process matters, but culture matters more. Every issue we surfaced traces back to either unclear ownership, slow escalation, or the absence of a shared vocabulary for risk. Fixing the process artifacts is the easy part. Building the muscle to surface bad news fast and metabolize it productively is the deeper, harder work. That's where leadership lives.

Stepping into calibration, the team has done a thoughtful job documenting impact and aligning ratings to the broader distribution curve. We want to be rigorous about differentiation — exceeds expectations should mean genuinely outsized impact relative to scope, not just hitting commitments. The conversation we're not having enough is around the tail: who is consistently below the bar, and what is the path to addressing it within ninety days.

The promotion case for the senior engineer is strong on technical depth but light on cross-functional influence. To level up, she needs to demonstrate consistent impact beyond her immediate team — driving architectural decisions across pods, mentoring up-and-comers, and shaping the engineering culture. The recommendation is to defer this cycle and revisit in six months with a clear development plan.

Calibration revealed inconsistency in how managers are applying the rubric, particularly for the senior individual contributor track. Some managers are anchoring on scope, others on craft, others on influence. We need a recalibration session with the people leaders to align on what good looks like at each level, otherwise we'll continue to see rating drift across the organization.

The performance conversation needs to be a two-way dialogue, not a one-directional pronouncement. Bring data, bring specifics, anchor on observed behaviors and outcomes, and create space for the employee to share their own reflection. The best development conversations leave the employee energized about the path forward, even when the feedback is critical. That's the standard we hold ourselves to.

We're seeing a healthy mix of ratings this cycle, with a meaningful long tail of high performers. Compensation actions will be tilted decisively toward this top quartile, consistent with our pay-for-performance philosophy. We need to ensure our highest contributors feel materially differentiated, because that's what protects against external poaching and signals what we value culturally.

Performance management is not an annual event; it's a continuous practice. The annual cycle is a forcing function for documentation and calibration, but the real impact happens in the weekly one-on-ones, the in-the-moment coaching, and the project retros. Managers who deliver clear, frequent feedback build teams that outperform. It's that simple, and that hard.

The performance improvement plan should be a serious, structured intervention with clear behavioral expectations, measurable outcomes, and weekly check-ins with the people partner. It's not a punitive measure; it's an honest investment in helping a colleague get back on track. If the plan succeeds, we keep great talent. If it doesn't, we've created a defensible record and given the employee genuine clarity.

Talent reviews this quarter highlighted several flight risks among our high-potential cohort. The pattern is consistent: ambitious early-career leaders who are hitting career velocity ceilings because the next role is currently filled. We need to architect internal mobility opportunities, stretch assignments, and lateral moves to keep them engaged, otherwise we'll see attrition we can't afford.

The 360 feedback came back with a consistent theme: incredibly strong execution, but the upward influence muscle needs development. The next eighteen months of growth depend on her being able to navigate the executive layer, build coalitions, and influence without authority. We're going to invest in executive coaching and pair her with a senior sponsor to accelerate that learning curve.

Calibration is fundamentally an exercise in organizational honesty. We owe it to our high performers to recognize them clearly and decisively. We owe it to the broader team to ensure ratings reflect actual impact, not tenure or proximity to leadership. And we owe it to our underperformers to be direct about where they stand and what needs to change. Anything less is a disservice to everyone.

We're building the operating system for the next generation of enterprise workflows, addressing a sixty-billion-dollar TAM with no clear category leader. Our wedge is a developer-first platform that lands bottom-up, monetizes through usage-based pricing, and expands into the enterprise via demonstrated value. The flywheel is product-led growth, fueled by an obsessive focus on time-to-value.

Our category is undergoing a generational platform shift, and we're positioned at the epicenter. The legacy incumbents are saddled with on-prem architectures, decade-old data models, and innovation cycles measured in years. We move in weeks, ship continuously, and have built our moat on a modern data foundation that competitors cannot replicate without a clean-sheet rebuild.

The team is the most important slide in this deck. Our founding team has shipped two prior products to nine-figure outcomes, knows this industry from the inside, and has personal conviction in the problem we're solving. Around the founders, we've assembled best-in-class operators from category-defining companies, each bringing pattern recognition and an extensive Rolodex of strategic relationships.

Our unit economics are best-in-class for this stage: payback under nine months, gross margins north of eighty percent, and a magic number above one. We have a clear line of sight to a billion in revenue with a path to GAAP profitability inside thirty-six months. The capital efficiency story is real and validated by the cohort data we'll walk through in the appendix.

We're raising forty million at a pre-money of two-fifty to capitalize the next two years of growth. The use of proceeds breaks down into hiring against our GTM engine, deepening the product moat with an AI-native capability layer, and prudent international expansion into the European market. We expect to be metrics-default-alive at the end of this runway with optionality to raise or not.

Our go-to-market motion is anchored on a high-velocity, product-led growth engine that converts free users into paid teams, then into enterprise contracts. The funnel is highly instrumented, conversion rates are improving cohort-over-cohort, and we have a repeatable playbook for landing the C-suite once we've earned credibility from the bottom up. This is a textbook PLG-to-enterprise motion.

Competitive dynamics in this space favor the technology leader with the cleanest data architecture. We've benchmarked rigorously against the field and consistently win on technical evaluation, time-to-value, and total cost of ownership. The product gap will only widen as we compound on our AI investments, because our data flywheel is already turning at a rate competitors will struggle to match.

Customer love is the leading indicator of category leadership. Our NPS sits at seventy-two, gross retention is best-in-class at ninety-six, and our net revenue retention runs above one-thirty. These metrics validate that we're solving a real problem in a way customers value enough to expand spend with us aggressively. Word-of-mouth is increasingly our most efficient acquisition channel.

Our long-range thesis is that every enterprise will rebuild its operational stack on AI-native primitives over the next decade, and the platform layer that emerges will be a generational franchise. We are building toward that platform from a position of conviction, with the team, capital, and customer momentum to actually win it. The market gets bigger the further out you look.

Risks are real and we want to be candid about them. Hyperscaler competitive risk, AI cost-curve volatility, and enterprise adoption velocity are the three we lose sleep over. Our mitigations include deep workflow integrations that create switching costs, a model-agnostic architecture that decouples us from any single AI provider, and a relentless focus on time-to-value to compress sales cycles.

The board convened to review Q3 performance, with the CEO walking through the operating dashboard and highlighting the meaningful expansion in ARR and the structural improvement in unit economics. Discussion centered on the appropriate level of investment behind our enterprise motion and whether we should accelerate hiring in international markets given the strong inbound demand signal. The board endorsed the proposed plan with minor refinements.

The CFO presented an updated three-statement model reflecting the latest forecast assumptions. Burn multiple has compressed materially, the path to default-alive is now ten quarters out at the current trajectory, and capital efficiency is trending into the top quartile of comparable companies. The board approved the revised budget and authorized the team to opportunistically raise non-dilutive growth capital if attractive terms surface.

The chair opened the audit committee discussion by reviewing the prior quarter's action items, all of which had been closed satisfactorily. The internal auditor presented findings from the cybersecurity review, noting that several legacy systems remained out of compliance with the updated information security framework. Management committed to a remediation plan with quarterly milestones and named the CISO as the executive sponsor.

Compensation committee reviewed the proposed equity refresh for the executive team, benchmarked against the latest peer-set data and consistent with our pay-for-performance philosophy. The committee approved the refresh as proposed, while encouraging management to broaden the long-term equity program one level deeper into the organization to better retain emerging leaders critical to the next phase of growth.

Strategic planning was the headline agenda item, with the leadership team presenting the refreshed three-year plan, the must-win battles, and the underlying capability investments required. Board feedback emphasized the need for sharper trade-off conversations and more explicit acknowledgment of what we are choosing not to do. Management will incorporate the feedback and recirculate the refined plan ahead of the next session.

Discussion turned to succession planning at the executive level, a standing agenda item that the board takes seriously. Management presented updated succession matrices for the CEO and CEO-minus-one roles, with named successors, readiness assessments, and development plans for each. The board commended the rigor of the process and asked for an enhanced focus on diverse pipeline development in the next iteration.

M&A pipeline review identified three actively monitored targets in adjacent categories. The corp dev team walked the board through the strategic rationale, integration thesis, and indicative valuation ranges for each. The board authorized management to advance exploratory discussions on the lead target while emphasizing valuation discipline and a clear bar for strategic and financial accretion.

The general counsel briefed the board on material litigation and regulatory matters. No items rose to the level of disclosable contingency, but management is monitoring an emerging regulatory framework in our European markets that could create compliance costs in future periods. The board acknowledged the briefing and requested a deep-dive at the next session with external counsel present.

Executive session was held at the conclusion of the formal agenda. The CEO joined for a portion to discuss organizational health, leadership team dynamics, and the talent agenda. The board provided constructive feedback on stakeholder communication and emphasized the importance of continuing to invest in executive bandwidth as the company scales into its next phase.

The meeting concluded with the chair summarizing key takeaways and action items. The board expressed confidence in the strategy, alignment around the operating priorities, and appreciation for the team's continued execution. The next regular meeting was confirmed, with a special session scheduled in six weeks to deep-dive on the international expansion plan ahead of fiscal year planning.

Walking through the H2 roadmap, we've sequenced initiatives to balance flagship feature delivery with platform investments that compound over time. The headline release lands in late October with the AI-powered workflow automation capability, followed by the enterprise security and governance pillar in December. We're being deliberate about not overloading the release train while still shipping meaningful customer value every six weeks.

The roadmap reflects the prioritization framework we aligned on last quarter: customer impact, strategic differentiation, and platform leverage. Every initiative passed through that lens, and several attractive ideas got cut because they didn't ladder up to the must-win battles. Saying no to good ideas is the hardest part of product strategy, but it's where focus actually gets created.

We have a notable dependency between the platform team and the workflow automation pod that needs careful sequencing. If the API contract isn't locked by end of August, the downstream launch slips by a full quarter. The recommendation is to elevate that dependency to a tier-one program with weekly executive visibility until we're past the integration risk window.

Customer-requested features are well-represented in the roadmap, but we're being intentional about not letting the loudest voices drown out the strategic bets. The right blend is roughly sixty percent customer-driven near-term wins, thirty percent platform investments, and ten percent horizon-three exploration. That allocation has tested well historically and we're holding to it.

The AI capability layer is the through-line that ties the next eighteen months of releases together. We're not building AI features as point solutions; we're building a horizontal capability that every product surface can compose against. That architectural choice has near-term cost in shared infrastructure investment but creates meaningful operating leverage as we scale.

Beta program kicks off in three weeks for the flagship capability, with twelve design-partner customers committed. The beta gates are quantitative and qualitative: usage thresholds, NPS targets, and a written commitment to be referenceable at GA. If we don't clear the bar, we extend beta rather than launching prematurely. Quality has to win out over schedule pressure.

Technical debt remediation is built into every sprint at twenty percent capacity allocation, non-negotiable. We've learned the hard way that under-investing in foundations creates compounding velocity drag. The teams that try to skip platform hygiene to ship more features end up shipping fewer features eighteen months later. Discipline upfront is operational leverage downstream.

We need to circle back on the international localization workstream. Current sequencing has it slipping to Q1, but the GTM team has committed to the EMEA expansion plan and a delayed launch undermines that bet. Recommendation is to pull forward localization by adding a small contractor team to backfill capacity, fully cost-justified by the projected pipeline impact.

Roadmap communications externally need a tightening. We're being asked the same questions repeatedly because the public narrative is too vague. The plan is to publish a refreshed product vision document, host quarterly roadmap webinars for customers, and seed our top accounts with the in-flight previews. Predictability and transparency build trust, especially as we move upmarket.

Net-net, the roadmap is well-architected, the prioritization is defensible, and the team is energized. There are real execution risks on the dependencies and a tight integration window, but the program management muscle has matured significantly and I have confidence in our ability to deliver. We'll reconvene in six weeks for the next checkpoint.

Our refreshed positioning anchors on three durable messaging pillars: time-to-value, total cost of ownership, and AI-native architecture. The narrative has been pressure-tested with twenty-five target customers and twelve industry analysts, and the resonance scores are meaningfully ahead of where we landed last cycle. We're ready to operationalize the new messaging across the full funnel.

Demand generation is shifting toward an account-based motion focused on the top five hundred named accounts. We're moving away from broad-reach digital toward orchestrated, multi-channel plays per account with sales and marketing on a shared scorecard. Early signal is encouraging: meetings-per-account up forty percent, opportunity conversion up significantly, pipeline quality measurably better.

Brand investment has been under-indexed historically, and we're correcting that. The category is becoming crowded and the customers we want to serve increasingly buy on trust, conviction, and category leadership signal. We're standing up a dedicated brand workstream, investing in thought leadership, and meaningfully growing our event presence to occupy the mindshare we deserve.

Content strategy is being re-architected around buyer journey stages rather than channel formats. We were generating high volumes of mid-funnel content with insufficient top-funnel awareness investment and almost no late-stage decision-maker assets. The refreshed model rebalances production capacity to where the actual buyer demand lives, with measurable lift in engagement and pipeline contribution.

Our category creation play is starting to gain traction. Three of the top analyst firms have validated the new category nomenclature, and we're seeing prospects use our language unprompted in discovery calls. The analyst-relations workstream has been the unsung hero here, and we're going to lean further in on third-party validation in the next quarter.

Marketing-sourced pipeline is up materially year-over-year, and our marketing-sourced ARR-to-spend ratio has improved to four-to-one, which is best-in-class for our stage. We're optimizing aggressively against this efficiency metric and re-allocating budget away from channels that don't clear the bar. Discipline at the channel level is what unlocks scale at the portfolio level.

Customer marketing is an underweight investment area we're correcting this half. Our existing customers are our most powerful advocates, and we've been under-leveraging them in advocacy programs, references, and community building. The refreshed plan stands up a dedicated customer marketing function with a clear scorecard around references, case studies, and net promoter score lift.

Field marketing budget is being concentrated on a smaller portfolio of higher-impact events. Last year we sponsored thirty-seven events with mixed-to-poor ROI; this year we're committing to twelve flagship moments with bespoke executive programs, curated customer attendance, and integrated pre- and post-event nurture. Quality over quantity is the operating principle.

Marketing technology stack consolidation is a multi-quarter effort that will simplify reporting, improve attribution, and reduce annual tooling spend by roughly twenty-two percent. The transition has some near-term friction but the operating leverage on the other side is substantial. We've named the program lead and the executive sponsor, and the project has clear gates and rollback criteria.

Net-net, marketing is in a strong position to be a meaningful contributor to the business this year. The team is well-architected, the strategy is sharp, the measurement is rigorous, and the partnership with sales is the strongest it's been in three years. We're going to keep our heads down, execute the plan, and let the results do the talking.

Three lessons from twenty years of scaling category-defining companies. First, the leader's calendar is the most honest signal of strategy: show me where you spend your time and I'll tell you what you actually prioritize. Second, talent density compounds; under-hiring at the senior level slows everything by a generation. Third, culture is the residue of the hard decisions you make under pressure. Build accordingly.

The companies winning this decade are the ones treating AI as an operating system rebuild, not a feature retrofit. Every workflow, every decision loop, every customer touchpoint is being reimagined from first principles. Executives who frame this as a productivity initiative are missing the magnitude of the shift. This is the new electricity, and we are at year one of a multi-decade reorganization of how work happens.

An honest reflection after my fifth board seat: the best directors ask the questions that make management uncomfortable in the most productive way possible. They challenge the strategy, stress-test the assumptions, and force the conversation no one else is willing to have. Comfortable boards build comfortable companies, and comfortable companies get displaced.

Unpopular opinion: most strategy work in big companies is actually budgeting in disguise. Real strategy involves making genuinely hard choices about what not to do, allocating resources asymmetrically, and tolerating the political consequences. If your strategy doesn't make anyone uncomfortable, you don't have a strategy — you have a five-year extrapolation of the current portfolio.

I get asked weekly how to build a high-performance culture. My answer keeps getting simpler: hire incredibly talented people, give them ambitious goals, get out of their way, and remove the ones who don't perform. Most cultural dysfunction in scaling companies traces back to leaders tolerating mediocrity for too long. Culture is what you walk past.

Thrilled to share that we've closed a fifty-million Series C led by a tier-one growth investor. This capital allows us to accelerate our category-defining mission, deepen our platform investments, and scale our world-class team across product, engineering, and go-to-market. To our customers: thank you for your conviction. To our team: this is just the beginning. The best is yet to come.

Leadership lesson from a difficult quarter: the best leaders run toward bad news, not away from it. They surface issues quickly, take ownership without flinching, and create the psychological safety for their teams to do the same. Information latency is one of the most expensive failure modes in any organization. Build the muscle to metabolize hard truths in real-time.

Three principles I share with every new manager: clarity is kindness, feedback is a gift, and direct is faster than nice. The cost of unclear communication compounds invisibly until you discover, eighteen months too late, that everyone was rowing in slightly different directions. Take the time to be explicit about expectations, outcomes, and trade-offs. It pays dividends.

Watching the AI shift unfold reminds me of the cloud transition fifteen years ago. The companies that won were not the ones with the cleverest demos but the ones that committed fully, rebuilt their operating models, and absorbed the short-term margin compression to capture the long-term platform position. The same pattern is playing out now. Half-measures will lose.

Concluding thought on the year. Building enduring companies is not about heroics; it is about boring, disciplined execution sustained over years. Show up, do the work, raise the bar incrementally, repeat. The compounding is invisible until suddenly it isn't. To everyone playing the long game: stay patient, stay hungry, and keep your eyes on the customer. The rest takes care of itself.

Based on our six-week diagnostic, we've identified three structural levers that, if pulled together, can unlock approximately one hundred and fifty basis points of EBITDA margin expansion over twenty-four months. The recommendations are rooted in industry benchmarking, transactional data analytics, and structured stakeholder interviews across the leadership team. We recommend a phased implementation with clear ownership and quarterly value tracking.

The portfolio review surfaced significant value-at-stake in two underperforming business units. Our recommendation is to pursue a structured divestiture process for one and an aggressive turnaround for the other, with clear gating criteria at the six-month mark. This sharpens the corporate portfolio, releases trapped capital, and concentrates management attention on the businesses with genuine right-to-win.

Our operating model assessment indicates meaningful opportunity to flatten the organization, collapse layers between the front line and the executive team, and clarify decision rights at every level. The current span-of-control averages four-point-two, well below benchmark; targeting seven-to-nine spans would meaningfully accelerate decision velocity and reduce the coordination tax that's currently throttling growth.

The procurement transformation has identified addressable spend of approximately three hundred million across indirect categories. A combination of demand consolidation, vendor rationalization, and renegotiation against benchmark pricing should yield seven-to-nine percent savings net of implementation cost. We've sequenced the categories to deliver early wins and build momentum for the more politically sensitive workstreams downstream.

Customer experience benchmarking against best-in-class peers reveals a meaningful gap in onboarding, particularly for the mid-market segment. The recommendation is to redesign the journey end-to-end, instrument every touchpoint, and embed customer-success specialists at the highest-leverage moments. We project this will lift first-year retention by six-to-eight points and materially expand lifetime value.

Our analysis indicates that the current pricing architecture is leaving meaningful value on the table, with willingness-to-pay surveys suggesting room to lift average realized price by eight-to-twelve percent on the enterprise tier. We recommend a structured price refresh, paired with rigorous deal-desk discipline and value-based selling enablement, to capture this opportunity without compromising win rates.

The sales force effectiveness study highlighted material variability in productivity across the AE population, with the top quintile generating four times the bookings of the bottom quintile despite comparable book quality. We recommend a multi-pronged intervention: refreshed enablement, performance management discipline, and a deliberate redeployment of accounts to align talent with strategic value.

Working capital optimization represents a near-term cash unlock opportunity. Days sales outstanding is roughly twelve days above sector benchmark, and inventory turns are well below peer median. A focused initiative across receivables collection, payment terms standardization, and inventory rationalization could release approximately eighty million in trapped cash with minimal disruption to operations.

The technology spend benchmark indicates the organization is over-indexed in legacy ERP customization while under-investing in modern data and AI capabilities. The recommendation is a deliberate reallocation: cap further investment in the legacy stack, accelerate cloud migration with a clear sunsetting roadmap, and stand up an AI center of excellence to centralize capability building.

In closing, the value creation thesis is supported by rigorous diagnostic, clear sequencing, and named accountability. The total economic prize approaches two hundred and twenty million in run-rate EBITDA over thirty-six months, with the bulk concentrated in the first eighteen. We recommend establishing a transformation office, weekly steering rhythm, and a granular tracking framework to ensure capture.

Three months in, integration planning is tracking ahead of the day-one schedule. The combined leadership team is in place, the integration management office is fully resourced, and we've established a clear cadence of weekly steering committee meetings to surface risks and unblock decisions. Synergy capture remains on plan, with revenue synergies trending modestly ahead and cost synergies fully baked into the FY26 operating budget.

Cultural integration is the workstream we are watching most carefully. The two organizations have meaningfully different operating cadences, decision rights, and risk appetites. We've invested heavily in shared offsites, leadership listening tours, and an integration culture charter that codifies the operating principles of the combined company. Early signal is constructive but we have a long road ahead.

Customer communication has been a particular focus. We've personally engaged the top one hundred accounts across both legacy customer bases, articulated the combined value proposition, and committed to seamless service continuity through the transition. Retention metrics on both sides remain healthy and the cross-sell pipeline is starting to materialize across the integrated portfolio.

Systems integration is on the critical path and we are working through the predictable complexity of harmonizing two ERP environments, two CRM platforms, and overlapping data lakes. The technology integration plan extends over eighteen months, sequenced to minimize business disruption while delivering the foundational data unification that unlocks the bulk of the operational synergies.

Talent retention remains paramount. We have identified the top two hundred critical-to-retain employees across both legacy organizations and have proactively engaged each through stay packages, accelerated career conversations, and direct exposure to senior leadership. Voluntary attrition among this cohort is below our threshold and the engagement scores are encouraging.

The procurement and supplier consolidation workstream is delivering ahead of plan, with renegotiated contracts already in place across the top twenty spend categories. We are seeing low-double-digit savings against legacy run-rate pricing, validating the synergy thesis articulated at deal announcement. Additional opportunities continue to surface as the workstream matures.

Brand and go-to-market unification is on track for the end of the second quarter. We've completed the brand architecture work, the field organizations have been redrawn into a unified geographic model, and the joint enablement program is live. The first integrated quota plans are being rolled out and early sales productivity indicators are constructive.

Regulatory clearance is fully behind us in our primary markets and we are nearing closure in the two remaining jurisdictions. The conditions imposed in those markets are manageable and have been factored into our operating plan. Compliance work continues in parallel and our legal and regulatory teams have done outstanding work to navigate a complex global approval process.

Risks we are actively managing include integration fatigue across the combined leadership team, customer concentration in the legacy book, and the residual complexity of dual operating models during the transition period. None of these are existential, but they require disciplined attention. The IMO is the air traffic control function ensuring nothing falls through the cracks.

Net-net, integration is proceeding well. The thesis remains intact, the team is executing with discipline, and the combined company is starting to operate as one. We remain confident in the value creation trajectory laid out at announcement and look forward to providing the next update at the upcoming investor day.

Dear shareholders: this past year was one of meaningful progress against our strategic priorities and continued investment in the durable capabilities that will define our next decade. We expanded our category leadership, deepened our customer relationships, and strengthened the operating muscle required to scale into a multi-billion-dollar franchise. I want to thank our customers, partners, colleagues, and shareholders for your continued conviction in our mission.

Our financial performance reflects the disciplined execution of a clear strategic playbook. Revenue grew at a healthy clip while operating margins expanded meaningfully, demonstrating the operating leverage inherent in our model. Free cash flow conversion improved, the balance sheet remains pristine, and we have substantial capacity to invest behind the highest-conviction opportunities in front of us.

Three themes defined the year. First, the acceleration of AI adoption across our customer base materially expanded the total addressable opportunity for our platform. Second, our investments in international expansion began to compound, with EMEA emerging as a meaningful contributor to growth. Third, the talent we attracted at the senior leadership level strengthened our ability to execute against an increasingly ambitious agenda.

We are entering the new fiscal year with confidence, conviction, and clear-eyed humility about the work ahead. The competitive landscape is evolving, customer expectations continue to rise, and the pace of technological change shows no signs of moderating. These are not obstacles; they are the conditions under which durable franchises are built and we are leaning into them with intentionality.

Our long-term financial framework remains unchanged. Over the medium term we expect to deliver durable double-digit organic revenue growth, continued operating margin expansion, and best-in-class free cash flow conversion. Capital allocation will continue to prioritize organic reinvestment, supplemented by disciplined inorganic activity where the strategic and financial logic clearly clears the hurdle.

I want to highlight the extraordinary work of our colleagues this year. They navigated a complex operating environment, shipped category-defining product capabilities, and continued to delight customers across every dimension of our business. Our culture of customer obsession, operational excellence, and intellectual honesty is our most enduring competitive advantage, and it lives in the daily choices of our team.

Sustainability and corporate responsibility remain integral to our long-term strategy. We made measurable progress against our climate commitments, expanded our supplier diversity programs, and continued to invest in workforce development. These are not philanthropic activities; they are strategic imperatives that strengthen our license to operate, attract top talent, and align with the values of our customers and communities.

Risk management deserves a clear-eyed word. The macro environment remains dynamic, geopolitical complexity is elevated, and the pace of technological change creates both opportunity and disruption risk. We have invested in our enterprise risk capability, stress-tested the operating plan against multiple scenarios, and maintained the financial flexibility to act with conviction across the cycle.

Governance remains a foundational priority. Our board of directors brings diverse expertise, deep industry knowledge, and unwavering commitment to long-term value creation. We are grateful for their counsel and stewardship. We thank our outgoing directors for their years of service and welcome the newly appointed members whose perspectives will further strengthen our governance.

In closing, we remain energized by the magnitude of the opportunity ahead and the privilege of serving customers who trust us with mission-critical work. We will continue to operate with discipline, invest with conviction, and execute with humility. Thank you for your continued partnership. Sincerely, on behalf of the entire leadership team.

Our agile transformation is now eighteen months in, and the operating leverage is starting to show up in the metrics. Lead time has compressed by forty percent, deployment frequency is up seven-fold, and change-failure rates are down materially. More importantly, the teams are owning outcomes rather than outputs, and the conversation about what to build has matured significantly across product, design, and engineering.

Scaling agile across the enterprise requires careful balance between team autonomy and platform consistency. We've adopted a federated model: small, empowered product teams operating on shared platforms with clearly defined contracts. The principle is autonomous within the lane, aligned across the highway. Premature standardization kills innovation; insufficient standardization creates integration nightmares downstream.

The shift from project to product thinking has been the highest-leverage change of the transformation. Project teams disband when scope is delivered; product teams own durable outcomes over multi-year horizons. The accountability is sharper, the institutional knowledge accrues, and the iteration cycles compound. This is not a process change; it is a fundamental rewiring of how value gets created.

Agile rituals are necessary but not sufficient. Daily standups, sprint reviews, and retrospectives are operating mechanisms, not the operating model itself. The deeper shift is in mindset: hypothesis-driven discovery, customer-centric prioritization, and a comfort with uncertainty. We've seen teams adopt the rituals while preserving the legacy culture, and the outcomes are predictably underwhelming.

Funding models need to evolve alongside the operating model. Annual project-based budgeting is fundamentally incompatible with continuous, hypothesis-driven product development. We're moving toward persistent team funding with quarterly investment reviews tied to outcome metrics rather than scope completion. The CFO partnership has been essential to making this stick.

Middle management has been the most challenging layer of the transformation. The traditional command-and-control role no longer applies, but the new role of coach, blocker-remover, and capability builder requires fundamentally different muscles. We're investing heavily in management capability building and being deliberate about replacing managers who cannot adapt to the new operating model.

Measurement has had to evolve. Velocity and story points are inputs, not outcomes. We've shifted the operating cadence to focus on flow metrics, customer outcomes, and business KPIs. Teams that previously optimized for sprint completion now optimize for value delivered, and the conversations in leadership reviews are radically more productive as a result.

Cross-functional dependencies remain the biggest source of velocity drag. We've worked hard to design teams around customer journeys rather than functional silos, but the legacy organization still creates hand-off friction in certain critical paths. The structural fix is to embed shared services directly into product pods where the integration is most critical.

The transformation has revealed uncomfortable truths about decision rights. Too many decisions still escalate to the leadership team that should be made closer to the customer. We've launched a decision-rights initiative to explicitly document who decides what at every level, with clear escalation criteria. Empowerment requires clarity, not just permission.

We are not finished with the transformation; we are not even close. The current state is a meaningfully better operating model than what we had, but the next horizon involves deeper customer integration, more sophisticated experimentation infrastructure, and embedding AI-augmented workflows into every product team. The compounding has just begun.

Our commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion is not a side initiative; it is integral to how we build a durable, high-performance organization. We've made measurable progress against our representation goals, but the data continues to highlight gaps at the senior leadership level that we are committed to closing through deliberate sponsorship, transparent promotion practices, and inclusive hiring at scale.

Equity is the operating principle that ties our DEI work together. Equal access to growth opportunities, fair compensation calibration, and transparent pathways to leadership are non-negotiable. We've invested in pay-equity analytics, sponsorship programs, and inclusive leadership training as the foundation. Behavior change at scale requires both the right systems and the right incentives.

Our employee resource groups have matured into strategic partners, not just affinity communities. They inform product decisions, drive recruiting initiatives, and provide candid feedback to leadership on the lived experience inside our company. We've increased ERG budget meaningfully and embedded leaders into our executive sponsorship structure to amplify their organizational impact.

Inclusive leadership is a learned capability, not an inherent trait. We've operationalized this through structured manager training, calibrated 360 feedback, and explicit inclusion criteria in performance evaluations. The teams led by inclusive leaders consistently outperform on engagement, retention, and innovation metrics, which is not coincidence — it is causation, and the data supports the investment.

Belonging is the leading indicator we track most closely. Engagement scores tell us how people feel about their work; belonging scores tell us whether people feel they can bring their full selves to it. The gap between aggregate engagement and belonging-among-underrepresented-groups is the most honest measure of our culture. We've made progress but we are not where we need to be.

Supplier diversity is a workstream we are formalizing this year. Our procurement team has set clear targets for spend with certified diverse suppliers, integrated diversity criteria into sourcing processes, and committed to public reporting on progress. This work strengthens our supply chain resilience while creating economic opportunity in the communities we operate within.

Accountability matters. We publish our representation data annually with the same rigor we apply to financial disclosures. We tie a portion of executive compensation to progress against our DEI commitments. We elevate the DEI conversation into every leadership forum because what gets measured and reviewed gets done. Performative DEI is the most corrosive failure mode and we will not engage in it.

Our hiring funnel has structurally improved through diverse slate requirements, inclusive job descriptions, and the use of structured interview rubrics that mitigate unconscious bias. Conversion rates from interview to offer are now equitable across demographic groups, which addresses a key leak point we identified two years ago. The work continues at the top of the funnel where representation gaps remain.

We acknowledge that progress is uneven and the broader macro environment has created headwinds for sustained DEI investment. Our commitment is unchanged. We will continue to publish data, hold leadership accountable, and resource the work appropriately. Difficult moments are when conviction is tested, and we choose to remain steadfast in our belief that diverse, equitable, inclusive workplaces are better workplaces.

Net-net, DEI is not a compliance exercise; it is a strategic imperative tied directly to talent, innovation, and customer outcomes. We will continue to integrate this work into our operating cadence, refine our approach based on data and feedback, and report transparently on progress. Thank you to every colleague who contributes to making this an inclusive place to do extraordinary work.

Welcome to our investor day. Over the next three hours, you'll hear directly from the leadership team about the durable thesis underpinning our business, the strategic priorities for the next three years, and the operating cadence we use to translate strategy into measurable outcomes. We are excited to share the depth of conviction behind our long-range plan and the discipline behind our capital allocation framework.

Our long-range financial algorithm centers on durable double-digit revenue growth, two-to-three points of annual operating margin expansion, and best-in-class free cash flow conversion. The composition is healthy: organic growth carrying the bulk of the headline, supplemented by disciplined inorganic activity, with operating leverage flowing through the model as we scale into our fixed cost base.

The total addressable market we serve continues to expand structurally. We size it today at approximately one hundred and twenty billion, growing high-single-digits annually, with our directly-addressable segment expanding faster as our platform extends into adjacent workflows. Our current penetration is in the low single digits, leaving substantial runway across cohorts, geographies, and use cases.

Our competitive moats are deep, durable, and compounding. Network effects in our data assets, switching costs embedded in mission-critical workflows, scale economics in our infrastructure, and proprietary AI capabilities trained on a corpus competitors cannot replicate. Each moat is meaningful on its own; together they create a competitive position that's exceptionally difficult to dislodge.

Capital allocation philosophy is straightforward: prioritize organic reinvestment in our highest-conviction bets, supplement with disciplined M&A where strategic and financial logic both clear the bar, and return excess capital to shareholders through opportunistic buybacks. The balance sheet remains a strategic asset and we will deploy it with the same rigor we apply to operating decisions.

Our enterprise motion has matured into a meaningful growth vector. Average contract values have doubled over twenty-four months, win rates against the most strategic competition continue to improve, and net retention in the enterprise cohort runs above one-thirty. We've made the investments — sales enablement, customer success, professional services — that this motion requires to scale durably.

International expansion is a multi-year growth story with sequencing discipline. EMEA is now run-rating at an attractive growth rate with operating leverage starting to flow. APAC is in the foundational investment phase with localization, regulatory readiness, and channel partnerships being established. We expect international to contribute disproportionately to growth in the back half of the long-range plan.

AI is both a tailwind and a transformative capability for our platform. We are operationalizing AI across every product surface, augmenting customer workflows, and embedding intelligence into our internal operating model. The investments are meaningful but the operating leverage on the other side is substantial, and we have line of sight to the use cases that translate into measurable business outcomes.

Our talent strategy is anchored on raising the bar with every hire, deepening our investment in development, and retaining our highest performers with differentiated equity and growth opportunities. We have meaningfully strengthened the leadership team over the past eighteen months and the bench is the deepest it's been in our history. Talent compounds, and we treat it as a strategic asset.

Closing thought: we are in the early innings of a generational opportunity, operating with conviction, executing with discipline, and investing for the long term. We thank our shareholders for your continued partnership. We look forward to the question-and-answer session and to engaging with each of you over the course of the day. The leadership team is energized about the path ahead.

Walking through the executive dashboard, the leading indicators across our north star metrics continue to trend in the right direction. Customer acquisition is healthy, activation rates have improved sequentially, and the cohort-level retention curves are flattening at higher levels than prior vintages. The lagging indicators are starting to validate the operational changes we made in the back half of last year.

Our magic number sits at one-point-two, putting us solidly in the efficient growth quadrant. Payback periods have compressed to nine months on the enterprise segment and twelve months on mid-market. These are the input metrics that compound into the durable LTV-to-CAC ratios we've committed to in our long-range plan. The operating muscle continues to mature.

Two metrics on the dashboard warrant deeper investigation. First, our self-serve conversion rate has been flat for three months despite increased top-funnel volume, suggesting friction in the activation flow that needs diagnosis. Second, gross retention in the SMB segment ticked down sixty basis points, which may be early signal of macro pressure on smaller customers. Both deserve a dedicated working session.

Net dollar retention is the metric I track most religiously. It captures the health of the existing book, the maturity of our cross-sell motion, and the underlying value perception. We're running at one-twenty-eight, which is best-in-class for our category and growth stage. The expansion architecture we built two years ago is paying off in compounding ways.

We need to instrument the leading indicators of customer health more rigorously. Right now we are too dependent on lagging metrics like churn and downsell, which means we are reactive rather than proactive. The proposal is to roll out a composite health score across the installed base, with intervention playbooks triggered by score deterioration. Customer success owns implementation.

Quarter-over-quarter improvement in deal velocity is notable. Sales cycle length is down eleven days on the enterprise motion and four days on mid-market. The driver is improved buyer enablement assets and tighter procurement engagement upstream. Velocity improvements at this scale flow through to multiple downstream KPIs and compound meaningfully over a full fiscal year.

Engineering velocity metrics have improved across deployment frequency, lead time, and change-failure rate.
